summary: Describes the IPv6 Jumbo Payload option, which allows packets larger than the normal limit, and the changes TCP and UDP need to use it. It replaced RFC 2147.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally packages have a maximum size. This allows an extra-large box for special fast links.

questions: how does udp length zero work
what is the maximum ipv6 payload size
subtitle: How IPv6 packets can carry more than 65,535 bytes of payload, and what TCP and UDP change to use them.

tldr.problem: The IPv6 header has a 16-bit Payload Length field, so a packet can carry at most 65,535 octets of payload. Links with a larger MTU could carry more, and UDP and TCP also have 16-bit limits.
tldr.mechanism: A Hop-by-Hop option called Jumbo Payload carries a 32-bit length, allowing payloads from 65,536 to 4,294,967,295 octets. The IPv6 Payload Length is set to zero, and UDP and TCP get small changes to cope with the larger sizes.
tldr.outcome: Only nodes that can attach to links with an MTU above 65,575 octets need to implement it. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2147 and reports no new known security concerns.

facts.label: IPv6 Payload Length in a jumbogram

today: RFC 2675 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1999. It obsoletes RFC 2147, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Jumbograms Exist
sections.content:
The IPv6 header has a 16-bit Payload Length field, so a normal packet can carry at most 65,535 octets of payload. A jumbogram is an IPv6 packet with a payload longer than that.

The RFC defines an IPv6 hop-by-hop option, the Jumbo Payload option, that carries a 32-bit length. That allows payloads between 65,536 and 4,294,967,295 octets.

The option matters only for nodes that may attach to links with a link MTU greater than 65,575 octets (65,535 plus the 40-octet IPv6 header). Nodes that cannot attach to such links need not implement or understand it. On a link with a configurable MTU, the MTU must not be set above 65,575 if some attached node lacks the option and it cannot be guaranteed that the option will not be sent to it.

The document merges two older sources: the option itself was part of RFC 1883, and the TCP and UDP changes were RFC 2147, which this document obsoletes. It also warns that the 16-bit checksum used by UDP and TCP becomes less accurate as the data grows.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal envelope only fits so many pages. Some special mail routes can carry giant boxes, so this document explains how to label a giant box.

sections.title: The Jumbo Payload Option Format
sections.content:
The option sits in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options header that comes immediately after the IPv6 header. It has an alignment requirement of 4n + 2.

It has three fields: Option Type, an 8-bit value of C2 in hexadecimal; Opt Data Len, an 8-bit value of 4; and Jumbo Payload Length, a 32-bit unsigned integer.

The Jumbo Payload Length is the length of the IPv6 packet in octets, excluding the IPv6 header but including the Hop-by-Hop Options header and any other extension headers. It must be greater than 65,535.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small sticker on the package that says exactly how big the package is, using a number big enough for giant boxes.

sections.title: Using the Option
sections.content:
The IPv6 Payload Length field must be set to zero in every packet that carries the Jumbo Payload option. A node that understands the option, on seeing a Payload Length of zero and a Next Header value of zero (a Hop-by-Hop Options header follows), with link-layer framing showing octets beyond the IPv6 header, must process that header to learn the real payload length.

The option must not be used in a packet that carries a Fragment header. Upper-layer protocols that use the IPv6 Payload Length to compute the Upper-Layer Packet Length in the checksum pseudo-header must use the Jumbo Payload Length instead for such packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The normal size box on the outside says zero, which means look at the sticker inside. Giant boxes also cannot be cut into pieces.

sections.title: Detecting Format Errors
sections.content:
Nodes that understand the option must detect several format errors. Unless the packet was destined to a multicast address, they report the error with an ICMP Parameter Problem message to the source. In all four cases the Code is 0.

  • Payload Length is 0, Next Header is Hop-by-Hop and the option is missing: the Pointer is the high-order octet of the IPv6 Payload Length.
  • Payload Length is not 0 but the option is present: the Pointer is the Option Type field.
  • The option is present and the Jumbo Payload Length is below 65,536: the Pointer is the high-order octet of the Jumbo Payload Length.
  • The option and a Fragment header are both present: the Pointer is the high-order octet of the Fragment header.

A node that does not understand the option follows the base IPv6 rules. For a zero Payload Length with a Hop-by-Hop header, it uses Code 0. For a nonzero Payload Length with the option present, it uses Code 2, with the Pointer at the Option Type field.
sections.plainLanguage: If the sticker and the outside label disagree, or the box is cut into pieces when it should not be, the receiver sends back a note saying what is wrong and where.

sections.title: UDP Jumbograms
sections.content:
The 16-bit Length field in the UDP header limits a UDP packet (header plus data) to 65,535 octets. The RFC relaxes this: a UDP packet longer than 65,535 octets is sent with the UDP Length field set to zero, and the receiver works out the real length from the IPv6 payload length. Before this change, zero was not a legal Length because the minimum is 8.

When sending, set Length to zero if and only if the UDP header plus data is greater than 65,535. Set the Jumbo Payload Length to the actual UDP length plus all extension headers between the IPv6 header and the UDP header. For the checksum pseudo-header, use the actual length, not zero.

When receiving, if and only if Length is zero, compute the length from the Jumbo Payload Length minus the extension headers in front of UDP. If Length is zero but no Jumbo Payload option is present, use the IPv6 Payload Length instead. Verify the checksum with the calculated length, not zero.
sections.plainLanguage: When a UDP box is too big to write its size, it writes zero, which means measure me from the outside label.

sections.title: TCP Jumbograms
sections.content:
TCP has no length field, but two things are limited to 16 bits: the negotiated MSS and the Urgent Pointer, which cannot reference data beyond 65,535 bytes.

For MSS, if the MTU of the directly attached interface minus 60 is greater than or equal to 65,535, send an MSS of 65,535. A received MSS of 65,535 is treated as infinity; the real MSS is the value found by Path MTU Discovery minus 60.

For the Urgent Pointer, the sender computes the offset from the Sequence Number. If it is under 65,535, it is used normally. If it is over 65,535 and at least the length of the TCP data, the Urgent field is set to 65,535. Otherwise the packet is split in two: the first piece gets an Urgent field of 65,535 to say the pointer lies beyond it, and the second piece carries the normal value. On receipt, an Urgent field of 65,535 with URG set means the pointer is at the end of the TCP data. The RFC also notes that larger windows are possible through the TCP Window Scale option.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP uses special numbers to say how big its pieces are. The value 65,535 is now a code that means as big as the road allows.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the Jumbo Payload option and TCP and UDP jumbograms do not introduce any known new security concerns. It says nothing more on the subject.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors did not find any new dangers from giant packages.

fields.name: Jumbo Payload Length
fields.desc: Packet length excluding the IPv6 header, must be greater than 65,535.
